headline: Stocks rebounded Monday on a tech rally, but the 10-year Treasury held at 5.00% and markets still price a December Fed hike going into Wednesday's decision.
dateline: Tuesday, October 27, 2026 · closes as of Mon Oct 26

rundown.h: Wall Street expects a hawkish hold on Wednesday.
rundown.p: CME FedWatch put the odds of no change Wednesday near 90% as of Monday. December is the live meeting: hike odds there range from about 73% to above 80% across reports. A Reuters poll found nearly 60% of economists expect the hiking cycle to peak at 4.00–4.25%. With no new dot plot, Chair Warsh's press conference carries the signal.

rundown.h: Buyers came back for two-year Treasurys.
rundown.p: Monday's two-year note auction sold at a 4.708% high yield, down from 4.787% at the prior two-year sale. The five-year auction follows today and the seven-year Thursday; the last five-year cleared at 5.033%. Treasury's quarterly refunding announcement on Nov 4 will show whether it plans to lean harder on longer-dated debt, a key input for the 10-year.

rundown.h: Anthropic's IPO filing puts real numbers on AI.
rundown.p: Anthropic's public S-1, for a Nasdaq listing under the ticker "ANT," showed $16.3 billion of revenue in the six months to June, versus $4.6 billion for all of 2025. It also showed an $80.7 billion net loss, mostly accounting charges, and a commitment to spend up to $120.5 billion on SpaceXAI computing through 2029. About a fifth of revenue came from two customers.

rundown.h: Meta wants up to $95 billion of new equity.
rundown.p: Meta plans to raise $35 billion through underwritten offerings, about $22.5 billion of Class A stock and $12.5 billion of preferred, then up to $60 billion more through an at-the-market program. Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom indicated they may buy up to $5 billion of the common. It's notable that a cash-rich giant is funding the AI buildout with stock, not just debt.

rundown.h: Microsoft offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees.
rundown.p: The voluntary offer covers roughly 27% of Microsoft's 223,000 workers, at vice-president level and below in the U.S., Canada, the UK and India. The company said it doesn't expect anywhere near that many to accept; an earlier round drew about 30% uptake. Microsoft reports quarterly results Wednesday after the close, alongside Alphabet, with Amazon on Thursday.

rundown.h: A U.S.–Canada deal may be getting closer.
rundown.p: White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett said Sunday the two countries are nearing an accord, and Reuters reported that relief from Section 232 steel and auto tariffs is under discussion. Politics is a factor: an AP-NORC poll found 64% of Americans say the president has gone too far on tariffs, and Axios reports Republicans are on the defensive a week before the midterms.

dive.title: The freight market is tight because the trucks are leaving
dive.dek: Diesel above $6, tougher enforcement and pricier insurance are pushing small carriers out, and rates are rising even though freight volumes have barely moved.
dive.body:
Truckload rates are climbing, but not because America is suddenly shipping a lot more stuff. It's because there are fewer trucks. FreightWaves' SONAR data put tender rejections, the share of contracted loads carriers turn down, near 14% in early October, roughly three times the 4–6% range of 2023–25. Over three years rejections are up 268% while truckload volume is up just 9%. Regionally it's sharper: 18.6% in the Midwest and 20.3% in the Northwest as of Oct 10, against 7.6% and 6.2% a year earlier.

The squeeze starts at the pump. AAA's diesel average hit a record of about $6.53 a gallon on Sept 21–22, up from about $3.70 a year earlier, and has stayed above $6 since early September. Small fleets pay for fuel within days but often wait 60–90 days to get paid for loads. At least 16 trucking and transport companies filed for bankruptcy between late August and Sept 21, mostly fleets of under 115 trucks. For-hire tractor counts fell by about 51,000 in August alone, and net authority revocations turned negative for the first time since at least 2019. Regulation adds to the drain: English-proficiency enforcement sidelines about 2,700 drivers a month, and a non-domiciled CDL rule could affect up to 194,000 over time.

Shippers are feeling it. Cass's truckload linehaul index rose 11.3% from a year earlier in August, the biggest gain since June 2022, while shipments rose just 2.1%, the first increase in 42 months. Dry-van contract rates averaged $2.69 a mile in the third quarter, up from $2.32 in 2024–25. Carriers aren't getting rich, though: the cushion between contract rates and non-fuel operating costs shrank to about 26 cents a mile in 2025 from about $1.01 in 2022.

For owners of truck yards and outdoor storage, it cuts both ways. Small carriers are a big share of that tenant base, and their credit is weakening. But tight capacity tends to push shippers toward drop trailers and extra yard space, and bigger fleets often scoop up the equipment of failed rivals. The picture would change fast if Hormuz reopened and diesel broke lower, if regulators eased enforcement, or if consumer demand cracked going into the holidays.

rows: Spot rate incl. fuel, per mile

items.title: October Dallas Fed survey: Texas factories' raw-material prices index hit 55.3, highest in two years
items.rel: Dallas Fed Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey, Oct

chart.t: Dallas Fed raw materials prices paid index (diffusion, SA)
chart.src: Source: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas via FRED (PRMSAMFRBDAL).

items.body:
The Dallas Fed's October survey of Texas manufacturers, released Monday, showed the general business activity index rising to 13.4 from 9.8 in September, against a series average of 0.3. Trading Economics had forecast 7; no consensus was published. The price gauges did the talking: raw materials prices paid rose to 55.3 from 52.2, nearly double its 28.1 long-run average and the highest reading since at least late 2024. Finished-goods prices received rose to 29.9 from 27.6.

Activity cooled underneath the headline. Production fell to 15.8 from 29.5 and new orders to 9.3 from 30.7, while employment eased to 11.6. Wages and benefits dropped to 20.8 from 27.4. Firms expect costs to keep rising: the six-month raw-materials outlook was 51.7. One transportation-equipment maker said fuel and domestic input costs are holding back a freight recovery.

The national picture matches. S&P Global's October flash PMI, out Oct 23, showed output prices at 59.8, the highest since August 2022, and the slowest supplier deliveries since July 2022.

experts.who: Chris Williamson, chief business economist, S&P Global Market Intelligence
experts.view: The renewed oil-price surge is feeding through to a wide range of goods and services, and supply bottlenecks and growing backlogs are making it easier for firms to pass on costs.
experts.src: Reuters via Galveston County Daily News · Oct 23

lead.title: Envoys converge on Tehran as Oman floats a Hormuz outline
lead.body:
Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's army chief Gen. Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iran's leaders in Tehran on Monday, a day after Qatari mediators arrived. The four countries agreed in a joint statement to keep talking about regional security. Oman said its own talks with Tehran produced an outline for a temporary arrangement to restore free navigation through Hormuz. Diplomats describe a Qatari package in which Iran reopens the strait and the U.S. lifts its blockade of Iranian ports; the sticking point is who goes first.

The ground hasn't caught up. The IRGC declared Hormuz closed Monday to vessels that don't comply with its rules, and the Houthis claimed new strikes on Saudi East-West pipeline pumping stations, which Riyadh hasn't confirmed. President Trump said it's "decision time" between a deal and finishing the war.
lead.reach: Through oil and shipping. Brent's December contract settled at $115.81 Monday (Oct 26), down 0.8%, and Hormuz is still handling about 4 transits a day against roughly 85 before the war, per IMF PortWatch data.

views.view: The navigation outline from Oman's talks with Iran could work, but only if both Washington and Tehran make compromises.

views.who: Fatih Birol, executive director, International Energy Agency
views.view: Even with diplomacy under way, energy markets are unlikely to return to pre-war conditions in 2027.

reading.title: Buffett's 2008 op-ed: buying into the panic
reading.dek: In October 2008, with markets in free fall, Warren Buffett told the world he was moving his personal money into U.S. stocks, and he was early.
reading.body:
Rewind to mid-October 2008. Banks were wobbling, credit markets had seized up, and the S&P 500 sat roughly 40% below its 2007 peak. Into that gloom, on Oct. 16, 2008, the New York Times published a short opinion piece from Warren Buffett with a title that doubled as a trade confirmation: Buy American. I Am.

The headline news was personal. Buffett explained that his own account, kept separate from the Berkshire Hathaway shares he had pledged to charity, had held nothing but U.S. government bonds. Now he was buying American stocks. And if prices stayed attractive, he said, his non-Berkshire net worth would soon be entirely in U.S. equities. For a famously patient investor, that was the financial equivalent of standing up in a quiet room and clapping.

What makes the piece worth rereading is how little it sugarcoated. Buffett called the financial situation a mess, at home and abroad. He predicted unemployment would keep rising and the headlines would stay frightening. He even admitted he had no idea whether stocks would be higher or lower a month or a year later. His bet was narrower and sturdier: markets tend to turn up well before the economy or the mood does, so waiting for good news usually means paying up for it. He also restated the rule he is best known for, about leaning in when everyone else is scared.

So how did the call age? In the short run, badly. The S&P 500 kept sliding, dropping roughly another 28% before bottoming on March 9, 2009, near 677. Anyone who followed him that week sat on a painful paper loss for months. But a year after the op-ed, the index was up about 20%, and the recession was later dated as ending in June 2009. One analysis found that $10,000 put into an S&P 500 index fund at the Oct. 17 close, with dividends reinvested, eventually grew more than elevenfold.

The lesson is not that Buffett nailed the bottom. He said plainly that he couldn't, and he didn't. The lesson is that price and mood are different things, and the gap between them is where long-term returns get made. The op-ed itself is short, plain-spoken and readable over one coffee. Find it in the New York Times opinion archive (it ran in print on Oct. 17, 2008), then pair it with Berkshire Hathaway's 2008 shareholder letter, written after the crash.

quote.text: Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful.
quote.src: Warren Buffett, "Buy American. I Am.", The New York Times, Oct. 16, 2008

takeaways: His rule cuts both ways: with the S&P near 7,680, ask who's greedy now.
